description: A large fridge egg needs 5 minutes 55 seconds for a medium egg: yolk set at the edge, soft inside. Times by size and altitude, from the Williams formula.

faqs.answer: Twenty-five seconds, for a large fridge egg: 5 minutes 30 seconds for jammy, 5 minutes 55 seconds for medium. The yolk edge passes from 68°C to 70°C quickly. A jammy yolk spreads; a medium yolk holds a soft slice.
faqs.question: What is the difference between jammy and medium?

faqs.answer: The yolk edge target: 70°C for medium, 84°C for hard. For a large fridge egg that is 5 minutes 55 seconds against 10 minutes 10 seconds. A medium yolk is soft in the middle; a hard yolk is set all the way through.
faqs.question: What is the difference between medium and hard-boiled?

faqs.answer: The edge of the yolk reaches 70°C, the top of the 65°C to 70°C range where Williams says yolk coagulates. Sources disagree a little on medium: some use 68°C and others go as high as 74°C. The 70°C used here keeps medium distinct from jammy without pushing into hard territory.
faqs.question: What temperature is a medium-boiled yolk?

faqs.answer: Longer, because the water boils cooler. At 5,000 feet the water boils at 94.9°C and a large fridge egg needs 6 minutes 50 seconds for medium, against 5 minutes 55 seconds at sea level.
faqs.question: How long is a medium egg at altitude?

faqs.answer: No. Deviled eggs need a fully set yolk that mashes smooth, and a medium yolk is still soft in the middle. Use the hard-boiled time instead: 10 minutes 10 seconds for a large fridge egg.
faqs.question: Can I use medium eggs for deviled eggs?

felicityNote: Medium is my weekday egg: firm enough to peel in a hurry, soft enough to enjoy. If jammy feels too fussy, this is your egg.

parts.meaning: The constant from the egg's thermal properties: density 1.038 g per cubic cm, specific heat 3.7, thermal conductivity 0.0054.
The weight of the egg in grams. A large egg is 57 g (USDA size).
The starting temperature of the egg: 4°C from the fridge, 20°C at room temperature.
The boiling point of the water: 100°C at sea level, lower at altitude.
The target temperature at the edge of the yolk: 70°C for medium.
The yolk edge factor. The yolk is about a third of the egg, so its edge sits about 69 percent of the way from the center to the shell.

formula.text: Time = 27 × M^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (Tegg - Twater) / (Tyolk - Twater)). For a large fridge egg at sea level, medium: 27 × 57^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (4 - 100) / (70 - 100)) = 356 seconds, about 5 minutes 55 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Boil the water first
howToSteps.text: Bring a saucepan of water to a full rolling boil. The formula assumes the egg goes into water that is already boiling.

howToSteps.name: Lower the eggs in
howToSteps.text: Lower each egg in gently on a spoon and start the timer at once. Keep the water at a gentle boil.

howToSteps.name: Time it
howToSteps.text: Boil a large fridge egg for 5 minutes 55 seconds. A medium egg needs 5 minutes 25 seconds, an extra-large 6 minutes 25 seconds, and a jumbo 6 minutes 50 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Cool it
howToSteps.text: Move the eggs to cold water for 5 minutes. This stops the cooking and keeps the center soft instead of setting firm.

howToSteps.name: Peel and slice
howToSteps.text: Tap the wide end and peel under cold running water. Slice with a sharp knife, wiping the blade between cuts for clean halves.

lede: A large egg straight from the fridge takes 5 minutes 55 seconds for a medium-boiled egg: the yolk is set at the edge and still soft in the center. The yolk edge reaches 70°C, the top of the range where yolk sets.

title: How Long to Boil Medium-Boiled Eggs
tutorial: Medium is the egg between jammy and hard: the yolk is set at the edge, soft and moist in the middle, and it slices without running. The yolk edge reaches 70°C, the top of the 65°C to 70°C range where Williams says yolk coagulates. For a large fridge egg that takes 5 minutes 55 seconds.

Medium sits close to jammy on the clock, only 25 seconds past it for a large fridge egg, because the yolk edge passes from 68°C to 70°C quickly once the heat reaches it. The difference is in the eating: a jammy yolk spreads, a medium yolk holds a soft slice. If your jammy eggs keep coming out softer than you want, medium is your setting.

Sources disagree a little on the medium target, and it is worth knowing the range. Some calculators use 68°C for medium, which is the jammy target here, and others go as high as 74°C. The 70°C used here is the top of the yolk setting range on Williams' own page, and it keeps medium distinct from jammy without pushing into hard territory.

Size and start move the time the usual way: a medium egg needs 5 minutes 25 seconds, a jumbo 6 minutes 50 seconds, and a room-temperature large egg 4 minutes 45 seconds. At 5,000 feet a large fridge egg needs 6 minutes 50 seconds, because the water boils at 94.9°C instead of 100°C.

Medium eggs are the all-rounders: good sliced over toast, good in a salad, good eaten plain with salt. They peel more easily than soft eggs because the white is fully firm, and they keep better than jammy eggs for the same reason. Give them a few minutes in cold water before peeling.
